title: Two Buttons, One Target: Fewest Presses | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: A big friendly calculator screen showing 3, with only two keys: '+1' and '×2'. Line 1: keys flash as random presses happen (3→6→7→14), screen wandering. Line 2: screen shows '90?'. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: A calculator with just two buttons. Can you reach ninety in as few presses as possible?
Most kids start pressing forward and get lost. There's a much smarter direction.
Hello, I'm Vantee! Let's crack this calculator.

scenes.visual: Question text left, calculator on the right (screen 3, keys '+1' and '×2'). Line 3: '+1' key glows. Line 4: '×2' key glows. Line 6: five choice chips 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.
lines: Here's the question.
A calculator shows three.
It has only two keys. One adds one to the number on the screen.
The other doubles the number on the screen.
What is the fewest number of key presses needed to make the screen show ninety?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Three fact cards appear one per line: 'start: 3', 'keys: +1, ×2', 'goal: 90 in the FEWEST presses'. The word FEWEST highlighted with Mark sweep on line 3.
lines: So what do we know? We start at three, and we want to end at ninety.
Each press either adds one, or doubles.
We don't just want a way to get there. We want the FEWEST presses.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; calculator and question visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: A vertical (or right-to-left) chain starting at 90 on the right. Line 2: undo-keys shown: '×2 undone = ÷2', '+1 undone = −1'. Line 3: rule card 'even → ÷2, odd → −1'. Line 4: 90 → 45 with arrow labeled ÷2.
lines: Welcome back! Here's the strategy: work backwards, from ninety down to three.
Going backwards, doubling becomes halving, and adding one becomes taking one away.
Halving is the big move, so halve whenever you can. If the number is odd, take one away first.
Ninety is even, so cut it in half. That gives forty-five.

scenes.visual: Continue the chain one arrow per spoken step: 45 →(−1) 44 →(÷2) 22 →(÷2) 11 →(−1) 10 →(÷2) 5 →(−1) 4 →(−1) 3. Halving arrows purple, minus-one arrows green. Line 5: the full chain read forward 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 22, 44, 45, 90, with the 8 arrows numbered 1–8 one by one. Line 6: answer badge '8 presses' with chime at end of line, choice C highlighted.
lines: Forty-five is odd, so take one away: forty-four. Halve it: twenty-two. Halve again: eleven.
Eleven is odd, so take one away: ten. Halve it: five.
Five is odd, take one away: four. Now four is even, but half of four is two, and that's below three!
So take one away instead. Four minus one is three. We made it!
Read it forwards from three: every arrow is one key press.
Now count the arrows, not the numbers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight.
Eight presses. That's Choice C!

scenes.visual: But can we beat 8? Line 2: row '3 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 96' in red with 'too big!'. Line 3: row '3 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 48', then '90 − 48 = 42'. Line 4: a +1 token travelling through two ×2 boxes and growing 1→2→4 (a 'snowball'). Line 5: value table: 'before all 4 doubles: 16, before 3: 8, before 2: 4, before 1: 2, at the end: 1'.
lines: Can anyone beat eight? Let's plan the doubles, and see why not.
Five doubles is too many. Three doubled five times is ninety-six, already past ninety.
With four doubles, three becomes forty-eight. We still need forty-two more.
Here's the trick. A plus-one pressed early gets doubled later, like a snowball.
A plus-one before all four doubles is worth sixteen. Before three doubles, eight. Then four, two, and one.

scenes.visual: Line 1: '42 = 16 + 16 + 8 + 2' with four +1 tokens. Line 2: try three tokens: '16 + 16 + 16 = 48' (too big, red), '16 + 16 + 8 = 40' (too small, red). Line 3: '4 doubles + 4 adds = 8 presses' boxed. Line 4: link to the forward chain 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 22, 44, 45, 90 with the four +1 arrows highlighted. Line 5: text 'Fewer doubles? Three doubles needs 9 adds: 12 presses.'.
lines: Make forty-two from those values: sixteen plus sixteen plus eight plus two. That's four adds.
Can three plus-one presses do it? The biggest three are sixteen, sixteen, sixteen: forty-eight, too big.
The next biggest is sixteen, sixteen, eight. That's forty, too small. Nothing in between!
So we need four doubles and four plus-one presses. That makes eight, and no fewer!
And it matches our chain: two plus-one presses at the start, one after the first double, one before the last.
With fewer doubles, it only gets worse. Three doubles would need nine adds. That's twelve presses.

scenes.visual: Two small cards side by side: 'Work backwards: find a path fast' and 'Plan the doubles: prove nothing is shorter'.
lines: When would you pick each way? Work backwards to find a short path fast.
Plan the doubles when you need to be sure nothing is shorter.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red with a one-line reason. Line 2: the chain 90…3 with its 9 numbers counted vs 8 arrows. Line 3: chips 6 and 7 crossed out with '4 doubles + 4 adds'. Line 4: chip 10 with note 'works, but not the fewest'.
lines: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
Choice D, nine, counts the numbers in the chain. But the presses are the arrows between them, one fewer.
Choices A and B, six and seven, are too few. We showed you need four doubles and four adds.
Choice E, ten, can reach ninety, but it isn't the fewest. Two presses wasted!
So here's a great habit. Count the steps, not the stops.
Ready for a challenge? Same calculator, same two keys, and it starts at three again.
This time, what's the fewest number of presses to reach one hundred?
Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Backward chain 100 →(÷2) 50 →(÷2) 25 →(−1) 24 →(÷2) 12 →(÷2) 6 →(÷2) 3, one arrow per spoken step. Line 3: arrows numbered 1–6, answer badge '6 presses' with chime. Line 4: '3 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 96, 100 − 96 = 4' and '6 presses' check row.
lines: Let's work backwards. One hundred, halve: fifty. Halve: twenty-five.
Twenty-five is odd, take one away: twenty-four. Then cut it in half three times: twelve, six, three!
Count the arrows: six presses.
Check: five doubles take three to ninety-six, and one snowball add-one makes the last four. Six presses!
Here's the sneaky part. The bigger target took fewer presses. If you got six, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: 'Work backwards: even → ÷2, odd → −1' and 'Count the arrows, not the numbers'.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
To reach a target with doubling and adding one, work backwards.
Cut it in half when it's even, unless that drops below the start.
Otherwise, take one away.
And count the presses, the arrows, not the numbers.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
